patient.name: Eleanor Matsumoto
patient.chief_complaint: Three-year progressive bilateral foot burning and numbness, poorly controlled diabetes
patient.hpi: Eleanor Matsumoto is a 59-year-old retired secretary with a 3-year history of bilateral foot burning, tingling, and numbness in the context of longstanding poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. She describes a constant burning sensation in both feet described as 'walking on hot coals,' worse at night, and notes numbness progressing from the toes to mid-foot. She has also developed bilateral lower leg numbness over the past year. She has had multiple diabetes-related complications: background diabetic retinopathy diagnosed 18 months ago requiring laser photocoagulation, and microalbuminuria identified 2 years ago. Her diabetes has been poorly controlled for over a decade — she has had HbA1c values ranging from 9-11% for years, with current HbA1c of 10.8%. She has been non-adherent with both diet and medications, attributing this to caring for her elderly mother. She denies alcohol use. She reports her feet have become numb enough that she burned the sole of her left foot on a hot bath mat last month without noticing it for several hours — she is alarmed by this sensory loss. Her primary care physician referred her after noting absent ankle reflexes and a foot ulcer scar on the left plantar surface.

report.overall_impression: Severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Sural and superficial peroneal SNAPs are absent bilaterally. Peroneal and tibial motor amplitudes markedly reduced with mildly slowed velocities. Upper extremity NCS relatively preserved. Needle EMG shows chronic active denervation in distal lower extremity musculature with sparing of proximal muscles. Findings are consistent with a length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Sural and superficial peroneal sensory responses absent bilaterally. 2. Peroneal and tibial motor CMAP amplitudes markedly reduced bilaterally with mildly slowed conduction velocities; upper extremity motor NCS within normal limits. 3. Needle EMG: chronic active denervation (fibrillations, long-duration polyphasic MUPs) in distal lower extremity musculature; proximal muscles unaffected. Findings are consistent with a severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy with a distal-predominant distribution. Clinical correlation recommended.

report.summary: QSART: bilateral feet absent (0 uL); bilateral lower legs severely reduced (0.08 uL). Heart rate variability: markedly reduced vagal modulation. Orthostatic vitals: BP 148/92 mmHg supine; 118/72 mmHg at 3 minutes standing; 112/68 mmHg at 5 minutes — orthostatic BP drop of 30/20 mmHg with symptoms. Findings indicate bilateral sudomotor failure in a distal-predominant distribution and cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction with orthostatic hypotension. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: duloxetine pregabalin diabetic neuropathic pain treatment guidelines

results.citation: AAN Guideline 2011: Treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy. Neurology 76:1758-1765.
results.summary: Duloxetine 60 mg/day: Level A evidence for PDPN. Pregabalin 300-600 mg/day: Level A evidence. Gabapentin 900-3600 mg/day: Level B. TCAs (amitriptyline, nortriptyline): Level B, avoid in elderly and cardiac disease. Opioids: avoid unless refractory to first-line. Topical capsaicin 8% patch: Level B.

output.summary: Duloxetine and pregabalin carry Level A evidence for painful diabetic polyneuropathy and are FDA-approved for this indication. Pregabalin is renally eliminated and dose adjustment is recommended in CKD (eGFR <30–60 depending on dose). Gabapentin also requires dose adjustment in renal impairment. Tricyclic antidepressants carry Level B evidence but have a less favorable safety profile in elderly patients and those with cardiac disease. NSAIDs are generally avoided in CKD due to risk of further renal impairment.
